scenes.say: A product page takes two hundred milliseconds to load. You will make it take two, and survive a payment that arrives twice without charging twice. First, why is it slow?
Today you will do three things. Check Redis before the database. Keep cached data fresh. And survive a payment message that arrives twice.
lines: Charge once, even if delivered twice

scenes.title: Slow product page
scenes.statement: A product page reads the database on every view. Make repeat views fast; 60 s of staleness is fine.
scenes.say: Start with a slow page. A product page reads the database on every view. For example, two hundred milliseconds each time. We want about two, from Redis, an in-memory store.

scenes.head: One product page read
scenes.say: One product page read: two hundred milliseconds from the database. Redis, which keeps data in memory, answers in about two. That's a hundred times faster.

scenes.head: A cache is a sticky note
scenes.say: You need one phone number all day. The library across town has it, but the drive takes five minutes. A sticky note on your monitor has it in five seconds. So the cache is the sticky note, and the database is the library.

scenes.head: Cache-aside: check, miss, fill
scenes.say: The app asks Redis first. Redis is empty, so that's a miss. The app reads the database, which costs two hundred milliseconds. Then it saves a copy in Redis, with a sixty second expiry timer, a T T L, short for time to live. The next request finds the copy: a hit, two milliseconds. This is cache-aside: the app manages the cache itself.

scenes.head: Cache-aside in code
scenes.say: In code, build a key, like product colon seven. Ask Redis. On a hit, return at once. On a miss, read the database, then save the price with set e x for sixty seconds. The loop calls it twice: a miss, then a hit.

panels.label: excerpt

scenes.say: Your turn. Same product, empty cache. Three requests arrive one after another. How many of them read the database? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Empty cache, 3 requests in a row. DB reads?

scenes.head: Three requests, one database read
scenes.say: One. The first request misses and fills Redis. The second hits. So does the third. Two hundred milliseconds, then two, then two.

scenes.head: The catch: stale data
scenes.say: Now the catch. Someone changes the price in the database to ninety dollars. Redis still holds one hundred. The next user hits the cache and sees the old price. That's stale data. It lasts until the T T L expires, at most sixty seconds. Cache-aside answers the slow page.

scenes.title: Stale sale price
scenes.statement: The price changed in the database, but the cache still holds the old one. One popular key expiring must not flatten the DB.
scenes.say: Next, a stale price. The database changed, Redis didn't. For example, ninety against one hundred. We want users to see ninety. Expiring a popular key must not crush the database.

scenes.head: Two cures for stale data
scenes.say: Picture a sale that ends at midnight. Redis keeps showing the sale price all morning. Cure one: peel the sticky note off when the number changes. That's invalidation. Cure two: stamp every note with an expiry date. That's the T T L, your safety net if a peel is ever missed.

scenes.head: Invalidation in code
scenes.say: Here's invalidation. Write the new price to the database first. Then delete the cached key. We warm the cache, and read a hit with the old price. After set price, the next read misses, reloads, and shows ninety dollars.

get_product(7)
print(*get_product(7))

scenes.say: Your turn. A popular key expires. Refilling takes two hundred milliseconds, and a thousand requests arrive meanwhile. How many reach the database? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Popular key expires; 1,000 requests in 200 ms. DB reads?

scenes.head: Cache stampede
scenes.say: About a thousand. Every request misses at the same moment, so every one runs the same query. That's a cache stampede, and the database Redis protected gets flattened. Fix one: let a single request refill while the rest wait. Fix two: add random jitter to each T T L, so keys don't all expire together.

scenes.head: More cache questions
scenes.say: Two more questions. Redis goes down? Fall back to the database, because a cache is never required. What to cache? Slow, popular, rarely changing data. That covers stale data and the stampede.
rows: Slow, popular, rarely changing; not exact data

scenes.title: Checkout hangs
scenes.statement: Checkout sends an email and builds an invoice before replying, so the page hangs. Reply fast, do the work later, even at noon peaks.
scenes.say: Now checkout freezes. For example, the page hangs while it sends an email and builds an invoice. We want an instant reply, and the work done later, even at noon.

scenes.head: A queue is a ticket rail
scenes.say: Picture checkout. You send an email and make an invoice, and the page hangs. A waiter pins a ticket on the rail and returns to the floor. Cooks take tickets at their own pace. The rail is the message queue.

scenes.head: Queue between API and workers
scenes.say: The API accepts the order, drops a job on the queue, and answers right away. A worker takes it and sends the email. A spike just makes the queue longer. Start more workers, and the backlog drains.

scenes.head: Respond now, work later
scenes.say: In code, a real broker, which stores jobs on disk, holds the queue. This in-memory one stands in for it. Checkout puts the order on the queue and returns two oh two Accepted: got it, not done yet. Later a worker takes the order off the queue and sends the email.

panels.code:
from queue import Queue
q = Queue()
def checkout(order):
    q.put(order)
    return "202 Accepted"
print(checkout(42))
print("emailing", q.get())

scenes.say: Your turn. Workers are down for an hour, so six hundred jobs pile up. Then the workers restart. What happens next? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 600 jobs queued, workers restart. What happens?

scenes.head: Workers down: jobs wait
scenes.say: The jobs drain, but first they wait. A durable queue stores every job safely while the workers are down. Six hundred pile up, and the API never slows. Workers return, and the backlog drains to zero. Nothing was lost. The queue answers the hang, but a job can now run twice.

scenes.title: Event delivered twice
scenes.statement: A payment_succeeded event can be delivered twice. Charge the customer exactly once, even if the worker crashes.
scenes.say: Last, the scary one: money. For example, event nine arrives twice, and the customer calls the bank. We want one charge, even if the worker crashes.

scenes.head: Where duplicates come from
scenes.say: Here's a favorite interview trap. The queue hands payment event nine to a worker. The worker charges the card. Then it crashes before sending the ack, the receipt that says done. No ack, so the queue assumes failure and delivers event nine again. That's at least once delivery: nothing is lost, but duplicates happen.

scenes.head: Idempotent consumer
scenes.say: The fix: an idempotent consumer, doing it twice equals doing it once. Every message carries a unique event id. Insert that id into a processed table, with the id as primary key. If the insert fails to add a row, we've seen it, so skip the charge. Only then ack. Event nine arrives twice, and charge prints once.

panels.label: excerpt
panels.code:
SQL = "INSERT INTO processed(id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING"
def handle(msg):
    with db:
        n = db.execute(SQL, (msg["id"],)).rowcount
        if n == 1:
            print("charge", msg["order"])
    ack(msg)
handle(evt)
handle(evt)

scenes.say: Your turn. Move ack above the charge, and the worker crashes right after the ack. What happens to event nine? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Ack moved above the charge, then a crash. Event nine?

scenes.head: Ack first: the payment vanishes
scenes.say: Never charged. The ack told the queue the job was done, so it deleted event nine. The worker died before charging, so no retry ever comes. That's at most once delivery, and it loses payments. So ack after the work.

scenes.head: Delivery guarantees
scenes.say: At most once: ack first, and a crash loses the job. Fine for metrics. At least once: ack after, so a crash brings a duplicate.
rows: metrics, where one loss is fine

scenes.head: Dedupe in two places
scenes.say: Exactly once across systems is hard, so dedupe twice. Your own database: a processed table, written in the same transaction. The card charge: an idempotency key, a label the payment A P I uses to ignore a repeat.
rows: processed table, same transaction as DB writes

scenes.head: A message that keeps failing
scenes.say: And a message that keeps failing? Retry with growing waits, called backoff. Still failing? Park it in a dead letter queue, a side queue. Together they stop one bad message from blocking the rest, and the processed table keeps the charge to once.

scenes.head: Say it: how caching works
scenes.say: Why cache? Repeat reads skip the slow database. So check Redis, an in-memory store, first. On a miss, read the database, then save a copy with a T T L. The next read is a hit.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Stale data? Delete the key on update. The T T L backs it up. Stampede? One request refills while the rest wait, plus jitter. Redis down? Fall back to the database.
rows: Delete the key on update; TTL is the safety net
One request refills; add TTL jitter
Fall back to the database; cache is optional

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Why a queue? The API answers fast, and workers do slow work later. Duplicates? Delivery is at least once: no ack means a retry. Exactly once? Not across systems. An idempotent consumer makes twice equal once. Ack before or after? After the work. A crash means a retry.
rows: Answer fast, work later, absorb spikes
At least once: no ack, retry. Dedupe on event id
After the work; a crash means a retry

scenes.say: Three exercises. Cache your slowest endpoint for sixty seconds, and log hit or miss. Send one payment event twice and prove only one charge happens. Kill a worker mid job and watch the message come back.
lines: Cache your slowest endpoint, TTL 60 s; log hits
Send one payment event twice: prove one charge
Kill a worker mid-job: watch the retry arrive

scenes.say: So say this. Cache-aside: check Redis, fill it on a miss. Set a T T L, and delete on change. Queues deliver at least once, so dedupe on event id.
lines: Check Redis; on a miss, fill it.
Set a TTL; delete the key on change.
Queues deliver at least once: dedupe on id.
